unit.title: Respond to guest related complaints and requests

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a guest request and a guest complaint?
options: A request asks for something; a complaint reports a problem
A request is always written; a complaint is always spoken aloud
A request comes from staff; a complaint comes from the guests
A request costs money; a complaint is always free to put right

questions.stem: Why should housekeeping staff welcome a guest's complaint?
options: It means the guest will leave a big tip
It gives staff a reason to stop work early
It is a chance to fix it and keep the guest
It proves that the supervisor is not doing the job

questions.stem: Which of these is a guest request, not a complaint?
options: "The shower has no hot water."
"There are ants on the counter."
"The sheets on my bed are stained."
"Could I have two extra pillows?"

questions.stem: A guest who complains and is then helped well is most likely to:
options: Come back and tell others about the good service
Never stay at any hotel in Jamaica ever again
Ask for the staff member to be dismissed
Leave the property without paying the bill

questions.stem: A guest stops you in the corridor and asks for extra towels. What should you do first?
options: Listen, then confirm the room and how many
Tell them to phone the front desk about it instead
Say that you are on your break and walk on
Give them towels taken from another guest's room

questions.stem: Why do you write each guest request in the housekeeping request log?
options: So that the guest can be charged for every request
So that you can show how busy you were that day
So the request is not forgotten and can be tracked
So the manager knows which guests are difficult

questions.stem: What should an entry in the request log include?
options: The guest's credit card and passport numbers
Room, request, time, who did it and when
Only the guest's name and what they look like
What you think of the way the guest behaved

questions.stem: A guest asks for an iron at 9 p.m. When should it be delivered?
options: The next morning, with the newspaper
Promptly, within the time the property sets
Only when you have finished all your rooms
Whenever the guest calls about it a second time

questions.stem: A guest asks for something the property does not have. What should you do?
options: Say yes, and hope that they forget about it
Say no and walk away without explaining
Tell them to buy it in town for themselves
Explain politely and offer another choice

questions.stem: A guest with a feather allergy asks for different pillows. What should you bring?
options: Hypoallergenic pillows with fresh pillowcases
Feather pillows taken from another guest room
The same pillows, turned over and plumped up
Extra blankets to use instead of pillows

questions.stem: A guest asks for a baby cot. After you set it up, what should you check?
options: That it is placed right next to the balcony door
That a pillow and a heavy blanket are in it
That it is clean, steady and locked open safely
That the guest pays for it in cash first

questions.stem: A guest asks for more toilet paper, soap and shampoo. Where should these come from?
options: From another guest's bathroom nearby
From the trolley or the linen store
From the shop in town, paid for by you
From the minibar in the guest's own room

questions.stem: You have delivered a guest's request. What should you do next?
options: Nothing more, because the job is done
Wait outside the room in case of a tip
Tell other guests what was delivered
Mark it done in the log, with the time

questions.stem: Before you enter a guest room to deliver a request, what should you do?
options: Open the door with your key and walk straight in
Call out the guest's name loudly down the corridor
Knock, say "Housekeeping", wait, then knock again
Push the item under the door and walk away

questions.stem: The door has a Do Not Disturb sign, but the guest asked for towels earlier. What should you do?
options: Knock loudly so that the guest hears you
Use your key and leave them on the bed
Do not knock; phone the room, as the rules say
Leave the towels on the floor outside the door

questions.stem: You knock, announce yourself and go in, and find the guest asleep. What should you do?
options: Wake them up to hand over the item
Leave quietly and come back later
Carry on cleaning very quietly
Turn on the lights so they wake slowly

questions.stem: A person in the corridor asks you to open a room, saying it is theirs. Why must you not open it?
options: Only managers are allowed to open guest doors
The room may not have been cleaned yet
The person may not be the registered guest
Opening doors is the job of maintenance

questions.stem: A guest starts to complain to you about her room. What should you do first?
options: Stop what you are doing and listen fully
Tell her straight away that it is not your fault
Explain the property's rules before she finishes
Call security to come and deal with her

questions.stem: Which body language shows the guest you are listening?
options: Arms folded and looking at your phone
Looking away and tapping your foot on the floor
Turning your back to carry on working
Facing the guest, eye contact and nodding

questions.stem: Which is a good apology to a guest whose room was not cleaned?
options: "I am sorry, Mrs Clarke. I will put this right now."
"That is not my section, so it is not my fault."
"We are short-staffed today, so you will have to wait."
"No other guests have complained about it."

questions.stem: What does it mean to show empathy to a guest who complains?
options: Agreeing with the guest that the hotel is terrible
Showing that you understand how the guest feels
Giving the guest a free night straight away
Telling the guest about your own problems

questions.stem: A guest is shouting in the lobby about noise from the next room. What should you do?
options: Stay calm, and invite the guest to a quieter place
Raise your voice so that the guest can hear you
Ignore the guest until they calm down by themselves
Laugh, to try to make the situation feel lighter

questions.stem: Why should you never argue with a guest who complains?
options: Because the guest is always right about every fact
Because arguing makes it worse and solves nothing
Because guests are allowed to fine staff who argue
Because the supervisor will do the arguing for you

questions.stem: After listening to a complaint, why do you repeat the main points back to the guest?
options: To check you have understood the problem
To make the guest say it all over again
To show the guest that they were wrong
To give yourself time to think of an excuse

questions.stem: A guest complains about something you cannot put right yourself. What should you do?
options: Tell the guest that nothing at all can be done
Promise a refund, to calm the guest down quickly
Tell the guest to write to head office
Tell the guest you will get your supervisor now

questions.stem: Who can usually offer a guest a refund, a discount or a free item?
options: Any room attendant who hears the guest's complaint
The guest who is making the complaint
The security officer who is on duty
A supervisor or manager with that authority

questions.stem: One way to remember how to handle a complaint is "LAST". What does it stand for?
options: Look, Ask, Smile, Tell
Leave, Avoid, Stop, Talk
Listen, Apologise, Solve, Thank
Log, Answer, Sign, Tidy up

questions.stem: You tell a guest the air conditioning will be repaired. What should you also tell them?
options: That it is probably their fault for using it
That maintenance never comes on time
That you will try, but cannot promise anything
When it will be fixed, and who will come

questions.stem: Why should you thank a guest for telling you about a problem?
options: Because you must thank everyone you speak to
Because it helped you find and fix a problem
Because the guest will then agree to pay more
Because thanking them stops them complaining

questions.stem: What does "following up" a complaint mean?
options: Writing the guest's name on a list of difficult guests
Following the guest around to keep an eye on them
Checking later that the guest is now satisfied
Asking the guest to fill in a second complaint form

questions.stem: A guest reports cockroaches in the bathroom. What should you do?
options: Spray insect killer over the guest's bed and luggage
Tell the guest that every tropical hotel has them
Squash them quietly and say nothing to anyone
Apologise, report it at once and offer a room move

questions.stem: A guest finds hair in the bath after the room was cleaned. What should you do?
options: Tell the guest that it must be their own hair
Apologise and re-clean the bathroom at once
Say that you will clean it again tomorrow
Give the guest a cloth so they can wipe it

questions.stem: A guest complains that the sheets are stained. What should you do with them?
options: Turn them over and make the bed again
Spray them with air freshener and leave
Leave them and give an extra blanket
Remake the bed with fresh linen

questions.stem: A guest reports a strong smell of gas in the villa kitchen. What should you do?
options: Light a match to find exactly where the leak is
Switch on the extractor fan to clear the smell
Spray air freshener and keep the windows shut
Open windows, use no flames or switches, get help

questions.stem: A guest complains about loud noise from a party in the next room. Who should you tell?
options: No one, as the noise will stop on its own
Your supervisor or security
The other guests, by banging on the wall
The police, before anyone else

questions.stem: A guest says that money is missing from the room. What should you do?
options: Search the guest's luggage to look for it
Report it to your supervisor and security
Tell the guest that they probably spent it
Say nothing, in case you are blamed for it

questions.stem: A guest complains that the water from the tap is brown. What should you do?
options: Tell the guest that it is safe to drink anyway
Run the tap until it clears, then leave
Apologise, offer bottled water and report it
Say that all the water in Jamaica is like that

questions.stem: A guest complains that a room attendant was rude to her. What should you do?
options: Defend your colleague and say the guest is wrong
Apologise, listen, and report it to the supervisor
Promise her that the colleague will be dismissed
Tell your colleague what the guest said about her

questions.stem: Why are guest complaints recorded in a log?
options: So that repeated problems can be found and fixed
So that guests who complain can be banned in future
So that staff can be blamed and punished
So that the property can charge for repairs

questions.stem: What should a complaint record include?
options: The guest, room, problem, action taken and outcome
Only the guest's name and the date
What the staff member thinks of the guest
The guest's passport and credit card numbers

questions.stem: While cleaning a checked-out room, you find a gold ring under the bed. What should you do?
options: Keep it for a week to see if the guest asks
Give it to the next guest who stays there
Hand it in to lost property and record it
Sell it, as the guest has already gone

questions.stem: A guest asks you which room her friend Mr Grant is staying in. What should you do?
options: Refer her politely to the front desk instead
Tell her the room, as she already knows his name
Take her up to his room yourself
Lend her your key so that she can find it

questions.stem: A guest's request was delivered late, and the guest is upset. What is the best response?
options: Explain that it was the guest's fault for asking late
Blame the colleague who forgot to pass it on
Apologise sincerely and stop it happening again
Say nothing and leave the item at the door

questions.stem: Which of these should be passed straight to maintenance (engineering)?
options: The guest wants more coffee sachets
The guest wants a late check-out
The guest wants a wake-up call
The toilet will not stop running

questions.stem: At the end of your shift, what should you do with any requests or complaints that are still open?
options: Hand them over to the next shift in the log
Leave them, as the guest will only ask again
Tell the guest that you are going home
Throw away the notes you made about them

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What is the manager in charge of the whole housekeeping department usually called?
What is the room on each floor where clean linen and guest supplies are kept called?
What is the evening service called, when the bed is turned back and the room is tidied for the night?
What is the name for guest supplies such as soap, shampoo and body lotion in the bathroom?
What is a guest who has stayed before and comes back again called?
What is the general word for the comments, good or bad, that guests give about their stay?
What is it called when a complaint is passed up to a supervisor or manager to deal with?
What is the form sent to maintenance, asking for a repair, usually called?
On a hotel item or service, what does the word "complimentary" mean?
What is it called when a guest is moved to a better room at no extra charge?
Which biting insect, which can spread dengue fever, do guests in Jamaica often complain about?
Name the small insects that often come in a line to food left out in a guest room.
Which two cleaning chemicals must never be mixed, because together they give off a poisonous gas?
What should you wear on your hands when you use cleaning chemicals to put a complaint right?
What do you put out to warn guests after you mop a floor?

essays.stem: Explain, step by step, how you would handle a guest's complaint from the moment the guest starts to speak until the matter is closed.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stop what I am doing, face the guest, make eye contact and listen without interrupting, so the guest feels heard. I stay calm and polite, even if the guest is angry. I show empathy, for example "I understand how frustrating that must be," and I apologise sincerely for the trouble, without blaming anyone. I repeat the main points back to check that I have understood, and I note the guest's name, room and the problem. Then I solve it: if I can fix it myself, such as bringing fresh towels, I do it at once; if not, I tell my supervisor or send a work order to maintenance. I tell the guest what will happen and roughly when. I thank the guest for telling us. Later I follow up to check that the guest is now happy. Last, I write the complaint, the action and the outcome in the complaint log.
markingPoints: Listens fully without interrupting; stays calm
Shows empathy and apologises sincerely without blaming
Checks understanding and notes the details
Solves it within own authority or refers it; tells the guest what will happen and when
Thanks the guest, follows up and records it in the log

essays.stem: Describe how you would deal with a guest's phone request for two extra pillows and a bottle of water, from receiving the call to closing it in the log.
essays.modelAnswer: I answer the phone politely with the department's greeting and my name. I listen to the request, then confirm it: the room number, two extra pillows and a bottle of water, and I ask if there is anything else and whether the guest has a feather allergy. I tell the guest how soon I will bring them. I write the request in the request log with the room, the items and the time received. I collect clean pillows with fresh pillowcases from the linen room and the water from the store. At the room, I knock, say "Housekeeping", wait, knock again, and when the guest opens the door I greet them by name and hand over the items. If they ask, I place the pillows on the bed. I ask if they need anything else and wish them a good evening. Then I mark the request done in the log with the time and my name.
markingPoints: Answers politely and confirms the room and request
Gives a time and logs the request
Collects the right clean items from the store
Knocks and announces; greets the guest and hands over the items
Offers more help and closes the log with the time and name

essays.stem: A guest is shouting at you in the lobby because his room has not been cleaned by 3 p.m. Describe how you would handle this.
essays.modelAnswer: I stay calm and do not raise my voice, take it personally or argue. I face the guest, keep an open posture and let him finish speaking. I invite him to a quieter place, away from other guests, if he is willing. I say, "I am very sorry, Mr Palmer. I understand you want to rest in a clean room." I check his room number quietly, without saying it aloud. I tell him what I will do: call my supervisor and the room attendant now, and have the room cleaned as soon as possible. I offer him somewhere comfortable to wait, such as the lounge or pool bar, if the property allows. I keep my promise and tell him when the room is ready. If he stays angry or threatens anyone, I call my supervisor at once. After the room is cleaned, I follow up to check he is satisfied, and I record the complaint in the log so the cause can be found.
markingPoints: Stays calm, does not argue, lets the guest finish
Moves to a quieter place if possible
Apologises and shows empathy; keeps the room number private
Takes action with the supervisor and gives a time; offers somewhere to wait
Escalates if needed, follows up and records it

essays.stem: Explain why complaints and requests are recorded, and what a good record should include.
essays.modelAnswer: Records make sure nothing is forgotten. When a request or complaint is written down, the next shift or the supervisor can see what is still open and finish it. Records show how quickly the team responds, so supervisors can see where service is slow. They show patterns: if many guests complain about the same air conditioner or the same room, the real cause can be found and fixed, not just the single complaint. Records also protect staff and the property if a guest complains again later or asks for compensation, because they show what was done and when. A good record includes the date and time, the guest's name and room, the request or complaint in the guest's words, who took it, what action was taken and by whom, the time it was finished, and the outcome, such as whether the guest was satisfied. Records about guests are kept private.
markingPoints: Nothing is forgotten; open items handed over between shifts
Shows response times and where service is slow
Shows repeated problems so the cause can be fixed
Protects staff and the property if there is a later dispute
Lists the contents: date, time, guest, room, issue, who, action, outcome (kept private)

essays.stem: Explain which complaints a room attendant can usually put right alone, and which must be passed on. Give examples and say why.
essays.modelAnswer: A room attendant can put right complaints that are part of their own job and within their authority. Examples are a bathroom that needs re-cleaning, stained sheets that need changing, missing towels, soap or toilet paper, or a bin that was not emptied. These should be fixed straight away. Some complaints must be passed on. Repairs, such as a leaking tap, a toilet that will not stop running, a broken air conditioner or a light that does not work, go to maintenance on a work order, because attendants are not trained or allowed to repair them. Noise from other guests and missing money or items go to the supervisor and security, because they may involve other guests or a crime. Complaints about staff behaviour, and any request for a refund, discount or free item, go to the supervisor or manager, who has the authority to decide. Safety problems, such as a gas smell, are reported at once.
markingPoints: Within the attendant's job: cleaning, linen and supplies, fixed at once
Repairs go to maintenance on a work order
Noise, theft or security go to supervisor and security
Staff behaviour and compensation go to the supervisor or manager
Explains why: training, authority and safety

essays.stem: A guest complains that the bathroom is dirty, with hair in the bath and a stained towel. Describe what you would do.
essays.modelAnswer: I apologise sincerely and thank the guest for telling me, without making excuses. I ask if this is a good time to clean, or whether the guest would like me to come back while they are out. I note the complaint and tell my supervisor. I take my trolley, gloves and the right cleaning products to the room, knock and announce myself. I remove the stained towel and all used towels and bring fresh ones. I re-clean the bath, basin, toilet, mirror and floor fully, using the products as the label and the SDS say, diluting correctly and never mixing them. I put out a wet floor sign if the floor is wet. I check every surface against the property's standard and ask my supervisor to inspect it if possible. I tell the guest it is done and ask if they are happy. Last, I record the complaint and the action, so the supervisor can check why the room was missed.
markingPoints: Apologises and thanks the guest; no excuses
Agrees a time and informs the supervisor
Replaces towels and re-cleans the whole bathroom to standard
Uses chemicals safely (gloves, label and SDS, dilute, never mix, wet floor sign)
Checks with the guest, has it inspected and records it

essays.stem: Explain how your body language and voice affect a guest who is complaining, and describe what you should and should not do.
essays.modelAnswer: When a guest complains, they notice how we stand and speak as much as what we say. Good body language calms the guest and shows we care, while poor body language can make them angrier. I should face the guest, stand up straight, keep my arms relaxed and open, make friendly eye contact and nod to show I am listening. I should keep a calm, steady and polite voice, not too loud or fast, and use the guest's title and surname. I should look concerned, not bored or amused. I should not fold my arms, put my hands on my hips, roll my eyes, look at my phone, turn away, laugh, sigh or tap my foot. I should not stand too close or point at the guest. I should not interrupt or raise my voice, even if the guest shouts. Good body language and voice help the guest trust that I will solve the problem.
markingPoints: Explains that body language and voice can calm or anger the guest
Should: face the guest, open posture, eye contact, nodding
Should: calm, polite tone; uses title and surname
Should not: fold arms, roll eyes, phone, laugh, turn away
Should not: interrupt, raise the voice or stand too close

essays.stem: A guest tells you that money and a watch are missing from her room. Describe what you would do and what you must not do.
essays.modelAnswer: I take the guest seriously, stay calm and say I am sorry this has happened. I do not accuse anyone, and I do not say she must have lost it. I report it at once to my supervisor and security, following the property's procedure. I do not search the guest's luggage or the room myself, and I do not touch or move things, because security may need to see the room as it is. I write down what the guest tells me: what is missing, when she last saw it, and who has been in the room, and I give this to security. If I cleaned the room, I tell my supervisor honestly what I did and when. I do not discuss the matter with other guests or staff who do not need to know. Security and the duty manager will decide whether to check the safe, the key records and call the police. Later, I help with any report.
markingPoints: Takes it seriously, stays calm and does not accuse anyone
Reports it at once to the supervisor and security
Does not search, touch or move things in the room
Notes the details and is honest about own visits to the room
Keeps it confidential and helps with the report; managers decide on the police

essays.stem: Describe how you would respond to requests from guests with special needs, such as a guest with a feather allergy, a family with a baby, or an older guest who walks with a stick.
essays.modelAnswer: I treat every special request seriously and politely, and I write it in the log so the whole team knows. For the guest with a feather allergy, I remove all feather pillows and duvets and bring hypoallergenic pillows and bedding with fresh covers, and I tell my supervisor so the room is noted for future stays. For the family with a baby, I bring a clean cot, check that it is steady and its sides are locked, and put no pillows or heavy blankets in it. I place it away from windows, cords and the balcony door. I can also bring a bottle warmer or a bath seat if the property has them. For the older guest who walks with a stick, I offer a room near the lift if the desk can arrange it, make sure the floor is dry and clear of trip hazards, place a non-slip mat in the bath and put items within easy reach. In each case I follow up to check the guest is comfortable.
markingPoints: Takes requests seriously, logs them and informs the team
Feather allergy: hypoallergenic pillows and bedding, noted for future stays
Baby: clean, stable cot, sides locked, no pillows or heavy blankets, safe position
Older guest: near the lift, clear dry floor, non-slip mat, items within reach
Follows up to check the guest is comfortable

essays.stem: Explain how the way staff handle complaints and requests affects the property's reputation and business.
essays.modelAnswer: Guests remember how they were treated when something went wrong. If staff listen, apologise and fix a problem quickly, many guests become more loyal than if nothing had gone wrong, and they come back and tell friends. If staff ignore a complaint, argue or forget a request, the guest feels let down and may leave early, ask for money back or never return. Today guests write online reviews from their phones, often before they even check out. One bad review about rude staff or a dirty room can be read by thousands of people and turn away future bookings, while good reviews that name helpful staff bring new guests. Following up, by calling or visiting the guest later to check they are happy, shows that we care and often turns a complaint into a good review. For villas and small properties, where many guests come back or are sent by friends, a good name is the main way to stay in business.
markingPoints: Good handling can make a guest more loyal; poor handling loses them
Repeat guests and word of mouth
Online reviews can bring or turn away many future guests
Follow-up shows care and can turn a complaint into praise
Links reputation to bookings, income and jobs

practical1.title: Role play: handle three guest complaints and complete the records
practical1.brief: In the Centre's mock guest room and a mock lobby, the assessor gives your group three guest complaint cards: (1) the bathroom was not cleaned properly; (2) the air conditioning is noisy and does not cool; (3) the guest feels a staff member was rude. Members take turns: for each complaint, one member is the housekeeping staff member, one plays the guest, and the others observe and take notes on a checklist. Each member must handle at least one complaint as staff, using the steps listen, apologise, solve and thank, and must do their own part of the paperwork. For each complaint, complete a complaint log entry; for complaint 2 also fill in a maintenance work order; for complaint 3, act out handing it over to the "supervisor" (the assessor). For complaint 1, actually re-clean the bathroom area of the mock room to standard. Photograph each stage below and add the photos, the log entries and the work order to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: Three complaint cards from the assessor
A mock guest room with a bathroom area, and a mock lobby
Cleaning trolley, gloves, cleaning cloths and the Centre's bathroom cleaning products, with their labels and SDS
Fresh towels and a wet floor sign
Blank complaint log sheets and maintenance work order forms
photos: Complaint 1: listening to the guest, facing them with open body language
The bathroom being re-cleaned, with gloves and a wet floor sign
The bathroom finished to standard, with fresh towels
Complaint 2: the completed maintenance work order
Complaint 3: handing over to the supervisor
All three completed complaint log entries
checklist: Listened without interrupting and kept calm, open body language
Showed empathy and apologised sincerely without blaming anyone
Repeated the problem back to check understanding
Took the right action within their authority, or referred it correctly
Told the guest what would happen and roughly when, and thanked them
Re-cleaned to standard using chemicals safely (gloves, label, dilution, wet floor sign)
Completed a log entry or work order fully and correctly
safety: Read the label and the SDS before using any cleaning product; dilute correctly
Never mix cleaning products, especially bleach and ammonia; wear gloves
Put out a wet floor sign and wipe up spills at once
Use only made-up guest names and details

practical2.title: Respond to guest requests: deliver and set up items in a guest room
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a set of request slips from the "front desk", for example: two hypoallergenic pillows for a guest with a feather allergy, a baby cot, an iron and ironing board, extra towels and bathroom amenities, and a late turndown. One room has a Do Not Disturb sign. As a group, log every request in the housekeeping request log, plan who will do what, and collect the right items from the Centre's linen store. Each member delivers at least one request: knock and announce, greet the "guest" (another member or the assessor), set up the item safely (for example, a cot that is steady with its sides locked and nothing loose inside), ask if anything else is needed, and close the request in the log with the time. Handle the Do Not Disturb room by the Centre's procedure. Photograph each stage below and add the photos and the completed request log to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A mock guest room with a bed, and a Do Not Disturb sign on one door
Hypoallergenic pillows and fresh pillowcases, towels and bathroom amenities
A baby cot, an iron and an ironing board
A housekeeping request log and pens
photos: The request log with every request written in
Items collected from the linen store
Knocking and announcing at the guest room door
The baby cot set up safely, sides locked, nothing loose inside
Hypoallergenic pillows placed on the bed
The iron and board set up safely, away from the bed
The request log with every request closed and timed
checklist: Logged the request correctly with the room, item and time
Knocked, announced "Housekeeping" and waited before entering
Respected the Do Not Disturb sign and followed the procedure
Set up the item safely and neatly
Spoke to the guest politely by title and surname and offered further help
Closed the request in the log with the time and their name
safety: Lift with bent knees and a straight back; get help with the cot and board
Check that the cot is steady with its sides locked, with no pillows or loose bedding inside
Set up the ironing board on a flat floor, away from the bed, with the cable out of walkways
Use only made-up guest names and details
